. Content signals and anchor texts already favour the home page, but there is a stronger and more general clue: the structure of the web itself. Thousands of pages link to the university home page, while only a handful link to a single course page. A hyperlink is an implicit recommendation: the author of the linking page considered the target worth visiting. The web is a directed graph with pages as nodes and links as edges, and its topology tells us which pages the web itself considers important.
This section develops two classic ways to read that graph.
computes one global importance score for every page, independent of any query. It was the key innovation of Google in 1998 and is still the reference model for ranking nodes in a graph.

distinguishes two roles that a page can play for a topic, hub or authority, and computes them on a small, query-specific subgraph. Both turn out to be the same mathematical idea: an eigenvector of a link matrix, computed by repeated matrix-vector multiplication.

This ranking matches our first intuition: E is clearly the centre of this graph. But look at B and G, which tie with four incoming links. G receives a link from E, the most important page. B receives its links from A, C, D, and F, which are all minor pages themselves. G should rank above B, because a recommendation from an important page should count more than a recommendation from an unimportant one. The in-degree treats all links as equal votes.
There is a second, more practical problem. In-degree is easy to manipulate. Anyone can create a thousand pages that all link to a target page, a practice called

, and inflate its in-degree at almost no cost. We need a measure in which a link is worth only as much as the page it comes from. Then a thousand links from a thousand worthless pages add up to very little.
PageRank, developed by Larry Page and Sergey Brin at Stanford, defines importance through a thought experiment. A
starts on some page and browses the web forever. On each page, the surfer does one of two things:

If a page has no outgoing links (a

), the surfer always jumps to a random page. The PageRank of a page is the long-run fraction of time the surfer spends on it. In terms of probability theory, the surfer performs a Markov chain with pages as states, and PageRank is the stationary distribution of this chain. A page with high PageRank is a page that people browsing the web would visit often, which makes it a good candidate for the top of a result list.

children.value: PageRank is not a relevance score

PageRank measures how often a random surfer visits a page. It does not know the query. A search engine computes PageRank once after each crawl and uses it as one feature among many, combined with content signals such as BM25F and proximity. Ranking by PageRank alone would return the same famous pages for every query. PageRank is therefore not “how relevant a page is”, but “how prominent a page is in the web graph”.

PageRank also favours old pages. A new page, however good, has not yet collected incoming links, and links from important pages take time to appear. This is one reason why search engines add freshness signals for news and events, where the best page may be only a few minutes old.

In 1998, Jon Kleinberg proposed a different reading of the link graph. He observed that pages play two distinct roles for a topic, shown in
is a page that the community recognizes as a definitive source on a topic, such as Wikipedia, IMDb, or the official site of an organization. Good authorities receive many links.
is a page that collects links to the authorities of a topic without providing much content itself, such as a curated list of resources or a directory. Good hubs have many outgoing links.

children.value: PageRank and HITS answer different questions. PageRank is computed once, offline, for the whole web, and measures global prominence regardless of the query. HITS is computed at query time on a few thousand pages and finds the best sources for one topic. This is also HITS’s main weakness: building and iterating a base graph for every query is expensive, and the topic focus is fragile, since a few strongly linked off-topic pages in the base set can take over the result. Web search engines adopted PageRank-style global scores. The hub and authority idea survived elsewhere. SALSA, a random-walk variant of HITS by Lempel and Moran, powered Twitter’s “Who to Follow” service, where the accounts closest to a user act as hubs and the accounts they follow act as authorities (
SALSA: hubs and authorities as a random walk (optional reading)

HITS sums the hub values of all linking pages and then normalizes. A hub passes its full value to every page it links to, however many links it has, and the principal eigenvector concentrates on the most densely linked group of pages in the base set. Lempel and Moran called this the

: a small group of pages that all link to each other can take over the result, even if the group is off topic. SALSA (Stochastic Approach for Link-Structure Analysis) replaces the sums with a random walk, in the spirit of PageRank.

Lempel and Moran showed that the stationary distribution of this walk has a closed form. Within each connected component of the graph, the authority value of a page is proportional to its in-degree, and the hub value to its out-degree. A dense community therefore gains only as much as it has links, and the iteration is not even necessary. The price is the mutual reinforcement of HITS: within a component, a link from a strong hub counts as much as a link from a weak one. SALSA is in effect an in-degree count on the query-specific base set. Its topic focus comes from the base set, not from the link weights.
On the eight-page base set of

, all pages form one component with 17 links, so each authority value is its in-degree divided by 17: D 35%, G 24%, C 18%, E 12%, B and F 6% each. The hub values follow the out-degrees: A 29%, F and H 18% each, B and G 12% each, D and E 6% each. The top two authorities agree with HITS, but C and E swap places. HITS ranks E above C because the strong hubs A and F link to E. SALSA ignores hub strength and ranks C above E, since it has three incoming links and E only two.

Early experiments with HITS revealed three problems. An entire domain linking to one external page creates an overpowered authority. Automatically generated links, such as advertisements or “site by” credits, grant authority to off-topic pages. And for a query such as “jaguar car”, the more frequent term dominates, so the top authorities are about cars in general rather than about Jaguar.
